title: Mastermind Options Intelligence — academic evidence ledger
scope: 18 primary academic/regulator research entries; public research only; no data analysis, production action, or external write performed by this worker
source_policy: Full-text availability is distinct from peer review and from complete methodological replication. Earlier drafts never silently substitute for final published tables.

papers.title: Option Volume and Stock Prices: Evidence on Where Informed Traders Trade
papers.access: Primary publisher abstract; full text not retrieved
papers.question: Can informed traders choose options and reveal information through trading activity?
papers.sample: Historical intraday equity/options observations; exact dates and selection criteria were not verified from accessible primary text.
papers.signal: Directional option-volume categories distinguish bullish combinations (call buys/put sales) from bearish combinations (put buys/call sales).
papers.horizon: Intraday lead–lag relations; exact lag grid not verified.
papers.result: The publisher abstract reports information in option activity about subsequent stock prices. No numerical effect is admitted here.
papers.controls: Theoretical endogenous trading-location model; complete empirical controls require full-text review.
papers.observability: Trade-side information is necessary; total call/put volume is a different observable.
papers.limitations: Foundational evidence, with incomplete methodological access in this pass; not evidence that every options feature leads equities.
papers.implication: Use as a directional-flow hypothesis and historical motivation, not a production calibration or priority claim.
papers.anchors: Published abstract; empirical-table audit remains open.

papers.title: The Information in Option Volume for Future Stock Prices
papers.access: Full published paper retrieved; targeted methods and results reviewed
papers.question: Does informed opening demand forecast stock returns?
papers.sample: CBOE non-market-maker volume, January 1990–December 2001; actual buy/sell, opening/closing, and investor-type categories.
papers.signal: Buyer-opening puts divided by buyer-opening puts plus calls; daily cross-sectional quintiles.
papers.horizon: Next trading day and next week, with subsequent decay examined.
papers.result: Low-ratio stocks outperform high-ratio stocks by over 40 basis points next day and over 1% next week on a risk-adjusted basis.
papers.controls: Market, size, value, momentum; information-asymmetry, leverage and liquidity comparisons.
papers.observability: The central signal uses nonpublic exchange classifications. Public quote-inferred trade direction does not recover opening status or investor identity.
papers.limitations: Publicly reconstructed flow predicts briefly then reverses; its incremental predictability disappears when the private component is included. Historical gross spreads are not current executable returns.
papers.implication: Label OPRA reconstructions as proxies. Require labeled-data validation before claiming replication of the headline result.
papers.anchors: Abstract; data section; public-versus-private volume analysis.

papers.title: Volatility Information Trading in the Option Market
papers.access: Full published paper retrieved; targeted methods and results reviewed
papers.question: Does option demand reveal future volatility?
papers.signal: Sum of signed call and put contracts weighted by vega/option price, approximating the derivative of log option price with respect to volatility; baseline maturities exceed one week.
papers.horizon: Individual future trading days at lags 1–5.
papers.result: Volatility demand positively predicts subsequent high–low-based realized-volatility measures after controls. No portable numerical forecast coefficient is asserted.
papers.controls: Implied volatility, lagged realized volatility, absolute delta imbalance, option/stock activity, and earnings specifications.
papers.observability: Actual non-market-maker buys and sells; Black–Scholes weighting uses volatility from the preceding 60 trading days.
papers.limitations: This is volatility demand, not a bullish/bearish score. Plain vega flow is a different feature; inferred aggressor side is not investor identity.
papers.implication: Preregister range/volatility endpoints separately and preserve the exact elasticity weighting as a named benchmark.

papers.title: The option to stock volume ratio and future returns
papers.access: Full published paper downloaded from author-hosted PDF; targeted sections reviewed
papers.question: Can unsigned relative option activity predict returns?
papers.sample: 1996–2010; 611,173 firm-weeks combining OptionMetrics, CRSP and Compustat.
papers.signal: Weekly option contracts across strikes, expiring within the 30-trading-day window beginning five days after trade, divided by equity volume in 100-share lots.
papers.horizon: Skip one trading day, then measure the following five trading days.
papers.result: Low-minus-high O/S decile four-factor alpha is approximately 0.34% per week in the historical sample.
papers.controls: Factor returns, stock characteristics, prior returns, separate activity measures and short-sale-cost comparisons.
papers.observability: Volume and contract definitions are observable; historical universe, adjustments and maturity filters must match.
papers.limitations: High O/S predicts lower returns in this specification. It excludes same-day expirations and does not justify treating all option activity as bullish.
papers.implication: A feasible public-data baseline, with original versus modern maturity buckets kept separate and borrowing conditions controlled.

papers.title: Why does the option to stock volume ratio predict stock returns?
papers.access: Primary institutional abstract and indexed publisher excerpts; full text not retrieved
papers.question: Which transactions explain O/S predictability?
papers.sample: ISE Open/Close Trade Profile observations; exact sample dates were not verified from accessible primary text.
papers.signal: Decomposition of relative volume into signed opening/closing transaction categories.
papers.horizon: Weekly stock-return predictability; precise skip/formation convention requires full-text verification.
papers.result: Opening call purchases are especially informative; closing call sales also contribute. Results do not support synthetic shorts being uniformly more informative than synthetic longs. No numerical magnitude admitted.
papers.controls: Accessible results compare trade categories and expiration weeks; complete regression specification remains unverified.
papers.observability: Exchange buy/sell and open/close classifications, not public aggregate volume alone.
papers.limitations: The decomposition challenges a single short-sale-friction explanation. Missing full text prevents a replication-grade specification.
papers.implication: Preserve transaction type and strategy ambiguity; do not substitute subsequent open-interest changes for observed opening intent.
papers.anchors: Institutional abstract and publisher indexed passages; table audit open.

papers.title: Deviations from Put-Call Parity and Stock Return Predictability
papers.publication: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 45(2), 335–367
papers.access: Published abstract plus full March 2007 working-paper version; final tables not retrieved
papers.question: Do relative call/put prices forecast returns?
papers.sample: Earlier draft: January 1996–December 2005. Do not assume every final-paper filter matches this version.
papers.signal: Open-interest-weighted call-minus-put implied volatility for matched strike/expiration pairs.
papers.result: Published abstract reports approximately 50 basis points per week between expensive-call and expensive-put portfolios and declining predictability over time.
papers.controls: Option versus equity liquidity; borrowing/rebate considerations. Final detailed specifications require final-text audit.
papers.observability: Paired option quotes, time-aligned stock price, valuation inputs and lag-appropriate open interest.
papers.limitations: Parity deviations can embed borrow costs and valuation conventions. Later evidence L17 materially qualifies the informational interpretation.
papers.implication: Build a borrow-aware relative-price feature and a temporal-decay test; do not translate the old spread directly into forecast probability.
papers.anchors: Published abstract; earlier working-paper data and signal definition.

papers.title: What Does the Individual Option Volatility Smirk Tell Us About Future Equity Returns?
papers.publication: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 45(3), 641–662
papers.access: Full author-hosted accepted manuscript retrieved; targeted sections reviewed
papers.question: Does downside option pricing identify weak future stocks?
papers.sample: January 1996–December 2005, OptionMetrics with equity, fundamentals and earnings data.
papers.signal: IV of an OTM put with K/S in 0.80–0.95 minus an ATM call with K/S in 0.95–1.05; choose contracts closest to 0.95 and 1.00, respectively; 10–60 calendar days to expiration.
papers.horizon: Weekly formation with a one-day skip; persistence beyond the next week is examined.
papers.result: Low-skew stocks outperform high-skew stocks by approximately 10.9% annually after risk adjustment in the manuscript.
papers.controls: Size, value, momentum, volatility, turnover, historical skewness, option activity and related option signals.
papers.observability: Quoted surface and positive open interest; matched clocks and contract filters matter.
papers.limitations: The variable combines information, downside-insurance demand and pricing frictions; it is not a calibrated physical crash probability.
papers.implication: Test incremental candidate deterioration after borrow, volatility and catalyst adjustment; maintain risk-premium versus information hypotheses.

papers.title: Expected Stock Returns and Variance Risk Premia
papers.access: Full published paper retrieved; targeted methods and results reviewed
papers.question: Does the aggregate price of variance risk predict equity returns?
papers.signal: Squared 30-day VIX minus preceding-month realized variance constructed from five-minute returns; both terms are observable at formation time. A forecast-based physical-variance alternative is also studied.
papers.horizon: Monthly through multi-year, with strongest principal evidence around one quarter.
papers.result: Quarterly regression adjusted R-squared is approximately 6.82%; higher variance premium predicts higher subsequent aggregate returns.
papers.controls: Valuation and macro-finance predictors; heteroskedasticity/overlap-robust inference.
papers.observability: Implied variance and already-realized variance on compatible scales; future realized variance is an outcome, not an available feature.
papers.limitations: Aggregate quarterly evidence does not establish next-day single-name direction. Variance and volatility spreads are distinct.
papers.implication: Use as a market-risk-state benchmark with an explicit horizon and unit contract, separate from short-term deterioration alerts.

papers.title: Tails, Fears, and Risk Premia
papers.access: Full published paper retrieved; targeted methods and results reviewed
papers.question: How much compensation reflects extreme-tail risk and changing fear?
papers.sample: High-frequency S&P futures, 1990–2008; index options, 1996–2008. Baseline estimation through June 2007 is applied to the later crisis interval.
papers.signal: Physical jump-tail estimates from high-frequency returns compared with risk-neutral tails from short-maturity deep-OTM option prices.
papers.horizon: Risk-premium decomposition and state variation, rather than a single next-day forecast target.
papers.result: Tail compensation is economically material and fear varies beyond ordinary volatility. No tradable-alpha estimate is claimed here.
papers.controls: Separate physical and risk-neutral measures, jump/continuous components and crisis comparisons.
papers.observability: Requires broad option tails plus high-frequency history; tail estimation extrapolates from more frequent movements.
papers.limitations: Sparse extremes and extrapolation assumptions matter. Risk-neutral tail prices include compensation and cannot be equated with physical event frequencies.
papers.implication: Expose downside-insurance state first; calibrate actual adverse-move probabilities separately on unseen outcomes.
papers.anchors: Tail estimation framework; empirical data and crisis analysis.

papers.title: Is there price discovery in equity options?
papers.access: Primary abstracts and indexed publisher methods passages; full text not retrieved
papers.question: Do option quotes add price information beyond current equities?
papers.sample: Tick-level quotes for 36 liquid U.S. stocks and three ETFs, April 17, 2003–October 18, 2006 (882 trading days), verified in indexed publisher text.
papers.signal: Disagreement between stock prices and option-implied stock prices from matched call/put quotes.
papers.result: The abstract finds no economically meaningful incremental option-price information; options adjust to the equity market. No numerical effect admitted.
papers.controls: Disagreement events are compared with similar control events; a larger, weaker-disagreement sample checks event-selection sensitivity. Complete filters still need full text.
papers.observability: Synchronized stock and options quotes with parity inputs.
papers.limitations: This null concerns a particular quote-level price-discovery question, not all future-return information in classified option flow.
papers.implication: Require quote-age, asynchronous-update and contemporaneous-stock baselines before calling option prices leading indicators.
papers.anchors: Publisher and institution abstracts; full-method audit open.

papers.title: On Inferring the Direction of Option Trades
papers.publication: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 38(4), 881–902
papers.access: Detailed primary publisher abstract; full text not retrieved
papers.question: How reliable are common option trade-signing rules?
papers.sample: Historical options with known true direction; exact dates not verified from accessible primary text.
papers.signal: Quote, Lee–Ready, Ellis–Michaely–O’Hara and tick-rule classifications.
papers.horizon: Trade classification, not a return forecast.
papers.result: Reported correct classifications are 83%, 80%, 77% and 59%, respectively, for each method’s classifiable subset; these are not identical-coverage comparisons.
papers.controls: Trade/quote location, size, moneyness, maturity, activity and complex index trades are examined.
papers.observability: True direction is needed for validation. Complex packages can make individual-leg execution prices misleading.
papers.limitations: Historical accuracy does not establish current vendor-feed accuracy. Excluding difficult observations changes coverage as well as accuracy.
papers.implication: Return sign probability, abstention and coverage; validate modern feed-specific calibration and retain a separate complex/ambiguous category.
papers.anchors: Published abstract numerical results and qualification by classified subset.

papers.title: The Price of Macroeconomic Uncertainty: Evidence from Daily Options
papers.publication: Federal Reserve International Finance Discussion Papers 1376
papers.access: Full regulator working paper retrieved; targeted methods and results reviewed
papers.question: How do options price scheduled macroeconomic uncertainty?
papers.sample: Daily S&P 500 option expirations, January 2017–May 2023; CPI, FOMC, payroll and GDP releases.
papers.signal: Insurance/variance and related premium measures for expirations spanning announcements versus nearby expirations without them; principal contracts have 7–21 calendar days remaining.
papers.horizon: Event insurance, evaluated before known releases; not necessarily same-day 0DTE trading.
papers.result: Options spanning important announcements command greater insurance premia; the effect varies with uncertainty and risk-aversion state. No numerical estimate admitted.
papers.controls: Adjacent expiry comparisons and alternative maturity, strike and event specifications.
papers.observability: Surface snapshots plus the event calendar as known at formation time.
papers.limitations: Priced uncertainty does not reveal the sign of the announcement surprise. Working-paper author findings are not Federal Reserve policy.
papers.implication: Make catalyst conditioning and event-specific variance normalization prerequisites for directional interpretations of elevated IV.
papers.anchors: Sample construction and treatment/control design; paper-page version metadata.

papers.title: Does 0DTE Options Trading Increase Volatility?
papers.publication: Working paper; presented at 2026 Conference on Financial Market Regulation
papers.access: Current author summary and primary conference agenda; full current manuscript not retrieved
papers.question: Does greater 0DTE trading raise underlying volatility?
papers.sample: Author chart covers January 2011–August 2023; the exact current estimation sample remains unverified.
papers.signal: 0DTE trading activity instrumented by staggered introduction of index weekly options.
papers.horizon: Underlying volatility; exact current outcome aggregation requires the full manuscript.
papers.result: Current author summary reports that a one-standard-deviation trading increase raises volatility by 9.10% of its mean, remaining positive after gamma-hedging controls.
papers.controls: Instrumental-variable design and market-maker gamma controls are stated; complete specifications not verified.
papers.observability: Trading volume is observable; causal interpretation requires instrument/exclusion-assumption review.
papers.limitations: Older circulating versions report different magnitudes. This entry uses only the current author summary and does not treat it as full-method verification.
papers.implication: Preserve an amplification hypothesis alongside L14–L15; compare estimands and regimes before resolving the apparent conflict.
papers.anchors: Author page updated August 2026; SEC May 7, 2026 agenda confirms presentation, not findings.

papers.authors: Adams, Dim, Eraker, Fontaine, Ornthanalai, and Vilkov
papers.title: Do S&P 500 Options Increase Market Volatility? Evidence from 0DTEs
papers.access: Full July 15, 2026 author-hosted manuscript retrieved; targeted methods and results reviewed
papers.question: How do expiring options and dealer positions affect intraday volatility?
papers.sample: January 2018–December 2024; baseline calendar identification ends May 19, 2022; classified Cboe activity and futures observations.
papers.signal: Presence of expiring contracts; market-maker gamma/hedging needs reconstructed from signed opening/closing histories, split into existing inventory and new trades.
papers.horizon: Ten-minute realized volatility and subsequent intraday intervals.
papers.result: Expiring-contract presence lowers ten-minute annualized realized volatility by 61 basis points on average. Earlier-established inventory drives the hedging shift, rather than new same-day positions.
papers.controls: Calendar variation and introduction comparisons; time effects; separate predictive intraday analysis is explicitly noncausal.
papers.observability: Exchange participant categories and position history, not a generic open-interest-times-gamma calculation.
papers.limitations: An average dampening effect does not rule out amplification in particular states. The manuscript supersedes two prior papers, which must not count as independent confirmations.
papers.implication: Keep starting inventory separate from fresh flow; test state-dependent intraday mechanisms without projecting them onto five-day stock direction.
papers.anchors: Title-page lineage; introduction; calendar design and inventory construction.

papers.title: 0DTE Index Options and Market Volatility: How Large is Their Impact?
papers.access: Full Cboe-hosted academic manuscript retrieved; targeted methods and results reviewed
papers.question: How large can measured dealer-gamma effects be?
papers.sample: July 2020–June 2023; proprietary Cboe SPX/SPXW transactions and intraday underlying data.
papers.signal: Market-maker inventory and gamma reconstructed using actual trade capacities; modeled hedging contribution to realized volatility.
papers.result: Typical positive gamma dampens volatility; negative-gamma episodes amplify it. The estimated largest daily increase is 3.3 annualized volatility percentage points in this sample.
papers.controls: Inventory-based regressions and a model counterfactual removing the gamma contribution.
papers.observability: Detailed participant-side transaction data and accumulated positions are central.
papers.limitations: The maximum is a model-dependent historical counterfactual, not a universal upper bound or experimentally identified causal estimate. Cboe data support and research funding are disclosed.
papers.implication: Use inventory uncertainty and state sensitivity, with explicit units; do not convert this estimate into a blanket safety claim about 0DTE.
papers.anchors: Abstract; sample and inventory construction; volatility-impact counterfactual.

papers.title: Hope at a Reasonable Price: Customer Use of Limit Orders in the 0DTE Market
papers.access: Full regulator working paper retrieved; targeted methods and results reviewed
papers.question: Can public data identify customer passive liquidity and execution costs?
papers.sample: SPXW, July 1, 2020–September 28, 2023; OPRA with proprietary Cboe transaction validation.
papers.signal: Customer limit-order presence from quote-condition codes, after correcting trade/quote sequencing problems.
papers.horizon: Trade-level execution and intraday customer liquidity provision.
papers.result: Customers frequently supply the best quotes; for actively traded slightly OTM contracts, their presence exceeds half the time in recent observations. No profitability claim about all retail traders follows.
papers.controls: Detailed trade/quote matching, sequencing reconstruction and participant-data comparisons.
papers.observability: Raw quote codes B/O/C identify customer interest at bid/offer/both when preserved; economic ordering can differ from naive timestamp sorting.
papers.limitations: Trade matching coverage is not side-classification accuracy. Reconstructing economic sequences must respect historical availability. DERA findings are authors’ views, not SEC policy.
papers.implication: Audit vendor quote conditions and sequence semantics before signing flow; passive counterparty must not automatically be labeled dealer.
papers.anchors: Abstract; sequencing problem and quote-condition methodology.

papers.title: Why does options market information predict stock returns?
papers.access: Current published abstract plus full March 15, 2022 precursor; final tables not retrieved
papers.question: Do familiar option-IV predictors embed borrowing costs?
papers.sample: 2022 precursor: July 2006–August 2015, Markit lending fees with OptionMetrics/CRSP. Final sample details require current full text.
papers.signal: Call–put IV spread and skew, related analytically and empirically to stock-borrow fees.
papers.horizon: Subsequent stock returns; monthly specifications inspected in the precursor, not asserted as the only final horizon.
papers.result: The October 2025 published abstract reports at least a two-thirds reduction in IV-spread/skew predictability after excluding high-fee stocks.
papers.controls: Borrow-fee adjustment and low-fee comparisons; earlier regressions also examine familiar return characteristics.
papers.observability: Contemporaneous borrow fees or clearly marked missingness; rates/dividends and pricing inputs must align.
papers.limitations: The result substantially qualifies L06–L07; it neither proves zero remaining information nor measures Mastermind’s candidate-risk utility.
papers.implication: Require borrow-conditioned incremental tests. A warning signal can retain decision value even when a short portfolio is uneconomic, but that value must be measured separately.
papers.anchors: Published abstract; 2022 precursor data and methodology; versions deliberately separated.

papers.title: Option Trading Activity, News Releases, and Stock Return Predictability
papers.access: Primary institutional published abstract; full text not retrieved
papers.question: Does news scheduling change which option transactions are informative?
papers.sample: Corporate-news and classified option-activity sample; exact dates and full filters not verified from accessible primary text.
papers.signal: Purchases versus sales of options, conditioned on scheduled/unscheduled announcements and timing relative to release.
papers.horizon: News days and periods before releases; exact windows require full text.
papers.result: Purchases are informative on news days and before unscheduled news, while pre-scheduled-release information appears in sales. No numerical effect admitted.
papers.controls: News scheduling and trading/margin-cost analyses are stated; complete specifications remain unverified.
papers.observability: Transaction categories and a point-in-time event/news calendar; future surprise labels are outcomes only.
papers.limitations: Missing full text prevents replication-grade implementation. The result rejects a uniform interpretation of elevated option purchases before known events.
papers.implication: Preregister event interactions and keep purchases/sales separate; avoid treating earnings-related option activity as automatic directional confirmation.
